blocks.text: Joshua’s repeated call to courage is not presented as mere fearlessness or force of personality. His courage and success are defined by Jehovah’s presence with him and by his continual meditation on and faithful observance of the law given through Moses. Leadership, therefore, is tied both to the promise that God will not forsake him and to the command that he not turn from the law.

sections.title: Rivers, Boundaries, and the Great Sea

blocks.text: The places named in the commission belong to several different geographic worlds. The Jordan is part of a Levantine river valley associated with boundary crossing, irrigation, and settlement, making the command to cross it a concrete movement into the land. The Euphrates belongs to Mesopotamian river geography, where irrigation, trade routes, and imperial boundaries shaped major powers. The “Great Sea” is the Mediterranean, connected with Phoenician trade, coastal routes, imperial movement, and Israel’s western boundary.

Joshua 1 begins the book’s movement through succession and entry, military campaigns, division of the land, tribal unity, farewell, and covenant renewal. These subjects define the book’s principal horizon; David, Solomon, the monarchy, exile, Jerusalem, and Samaria are not its main people, events, or settings.
